subject: Biology
title: Ecosystem
summary: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with the physical environment. Its structure includes species composition and stratification.

Its functions: productivity, decomposition, energy flow and nutrient cycling. Energy flow is unidirectional, from the sun through producers to consumers; only about 10% passes to each next trophic level (Lindeman's 10% law).
Ecological pyramids (number, biomass, energy) show trophic structure; the energy pyramid is always upright.
Ecological succession turns bare areas (primary) or disturbed areas (secondary) into climax communities through seral stages.

formulas.name: Productivity
formulas.formula: primary productivity = rate of biomass (organic matter) produced per unit area over time by plants in photosynthesis (g m⁻² yr⁻¹ or kcal m⁻² yr⁻¹);  GPP = rate of production of organic matter during photosynthesis;  NPP = GPP − R (R = respiration losses) = biomass available to heterotrophs (herbivores, decomposers);  secondary productivity = rate of new organic matter formed by consumers

formulas.name: World productivity
formulas.formula: annual NPP of biosphere ≈ 170 billion tons (dry weight);  oceans (70% of surface) ≈ 55 billion tons

formulas.name: PAR
formulas.formula: plants capture only 2–10% of photosynthetically active radiation (PAR), which is less than 50% of incident solar radiation

formulas.name: Ten per cent law
formulas.formula: only about 10% of energy passes from one trophic level to the next (Lindeman, 1942)

formulas.name: Decomposition steps
formulas.formula: fragmentation (detritivores, earthworm) → leaching (water-soluble nutrients into soil) → catabolism (enzymes of bacteria and fungi) → humification (humus — dark, amorphous, resistant, colloidal) → mineralisation (release of inorganic nutrients)

formulas.name: Factors affecting decomposition
formulas.formula: faster when detritus is rich in nitrogen and water-soluble sugars, in warm and moist conditions;  slower with lignin and chitin, low temperature, anaerobiosis

formulas.name: Food chains
formulas.formula: grazing food chain (GFC): grass → goat → man;  detritus food chain (DFC): begins with dead organic matter — decomposers (saprotrophs)
formulas.note: In aquatic ecosystems GFC is the major conduit for energy; in terrestrial ecosystems far more energy flows through DFC.

formulas.name: Trophic levels
formulas.formula: producers (1st) → primary consumers/herbivores (2nd) → secondary consumers (3rd) → tertiary consumers (4th)

formulas.name: Ecological pyramids
formulas.formula: number: upright in grassland, inverted for a tree;  biomass: upright on land, inverted in sea (phytoplankton less than fish);  energy: always upright

formulas.name: Standing crop and state
formulas.formula: standing crop = mass of living material at a trophic level at a particular time;  standing state = amount of nutrients present in the soil at any given time

formulas.name: Succession
formulas.formula: pioneer species → seral communities (seres) → climax community;  hydrarch (in water): phytoplankton → submerged plants → floating → reed swamp → marsh-meadow → scrub → forest;  xerarch (dry): lichens → mosses → herbs → shrubs → trees

formulas.name: Primary vs secondary succession
formulas.formula: primary: bare area with no soil (newly cooled lava, bare rock) — slow, hundreds to thousands of years;  secondary: after natural vegetation is lost (abandoned farmland, burned or cut forests) — faster because soil is present

formulas.name: Nutrient cycles
formulas.formula: gaseous (reservoir in atmosphere — nitrogen, carbon);  sedimentary (reservoir in Earth's crust — phosphorus, sulphur)

examples.title: NPP
examples.problem: GPP of an ecosystem is 100 kcal/m²/yr and respiration losses are 20 kcal/m²/yr. NPP?

examples.title: Energy to tertiary consumers
examples.problem: Producers fix 10,000 J. How much reaches tertiary consumers by the 10% law?

examples.title: Inverted pyramid of biomass
examples.problem: Why is the pyramid of biomass inverted in the sea?
examples.solution: Phytoplankton have a small standing biomass at any moment but reproduce very fast; the fish that eat them have a larger biomass.

examples.title: Pioneers on rock
examples.problem: Why are lichens the pioneers on bare rock?
examples.solution: They secrete acids that dissolve rock, helping weathering and soil formation, which later allows mosses and other plants to grow.

examples.title: Carbon cycle fact
examples.problem: What fraction of the dry weight of organisms is carbon, and where is most carbon stored?
examples.solution: About 49% of the dry weight of organisms is carbon. Oceans hold about 71% of global carbon as dissolved carbon.

topics.title: Ecosystem structure
topics.explain: Biotic components: producers, consumers, decomposers. Abiotic: light, temperature, water, soil. Vertical distribution of species at different levels is called stratification (trees top, shrubs, herbs and grasses bottom in forests).

topics.title: Phosphorus cycle
topics.explain: Rocks are the main reservoir of phosphorus as phosphates; weathering releases them into soil, plants absorb them, and decomposers return phosphorus to the soil. There is no significant respiratory release of phosphorus into the atmosphere, unlike carbon.

topics.title: Carbon cycle
topics.explain: Producers fix about 4 × 10¹³ kg of carbon annually through photosynthesis. Carbon returns to the atmosphere through respiration, decomposition, burning of fossil fuels and wood, forest fires and volcanic activity. Human activity has increased atmospheric CO₂.

topics.title: Ecosystem services
topics.explain: Healthy ecosystems purify air and water, mitigate floods and droughts, cycle nutrients, generate fertile soils, provide habitat, pollinate flowers and store carbon. Robert Constanza estimated nature's services at about US $33 trillion per year — nearly twice the global gross national product.

topics.title: Limitations of ecological pyramids
topics.explain: They don't consider the same species belonging to two or more trophic levels, they assume a simple food chain (not a food web) and saprophytes are not given any place in them even though they play a vital role.

topics.title: Climax community
topics.explain: The final, stable community in equilibrium with the environment. All succession — in water or on land — tends towards a medium-water (mesic) climax.

ratta: Energy pyramid always upright;  biomass inverted in sea;  number inverted for a tree.
Hydrarch: phytoplankton → … → forest;  xerarch: lichens first.
P cycle: sedimentary (rocks);  C cycle: gaseous.
GPP = rate of organic matter made in photosynthesis;  NPP = GPP − R, left for heterotrophs.
Ecosystems are NOT exempt from the 2nd law of thermodynamics — they need a constant energy supply to build molecules and counter rising disorder (entropy).
